papers.source_body_en: An outbreak investigation of influenza was conducted in a school in Phrai Bueng District, Sisaket Province, during 13 February–3 March 2025. The objective were to confirm the diagnosis and the existence of the outbreak, characterize the magnitude of the problem and describe the distribution of cases by person, time, and place, identify the source of infection and modes of transmission, analyze risk factors among exposed individuals as well as protective factors and ultimately, to implement appropriate prevention and control measures. A descriptive epidemiological study was carried out by reviewing medical records and conducting active case finding through interviews with students and school staff. An analytical epidemiological study was performed to identify risk and protective factors among cases and controls. using a case–control study and Chi-square test, and Environmental assessment and laboratory investigations were also conducted. A total of 43 cases meeting the influenza case definition were identified, with an attack rate of 25.59%. The median age of cases was 11 years, and the male-to-female ratio was 1:1.38. Influenza A/B antigen rapid tests were positive for Influenza A in 3 cases, and real-time RT-PCR detected Influenza A/H3N2 viral RNA in 2 cases. A statistically significant protective factor was maintaining a distance of at least 1 meter between desks in classrooms (adj OR = 0.19, 95% CI: 0.06–0.58, p-value = 0.005). This study demonstrates that physical distancing, particularly in classroom settings, is an effective measure for reducing influenza transmission in schools. Following the implementation of control measures, the last case was reported on 25 February 2025, and no additional cases were identified during 7 days of continued surveillance.

papers.title: Hematologic and biochemical prognostic indicators of influenza disease severity in naïve and preimmune ferret (Mustela putorius furo) models
papers.abstract: Abstract Ferrets ( Mustela putorius furo ) are widely used to evaluate influenza virus pathogenicity and pandemic risk, but hematologic and biochemical parameters are not routinely included in these assessments. In this study, we performed a comparative analysis of complete blood count and serum chemistry profiles in immunologically naïve and preimmune ferrets following intranasal inoculation with different influenza virus strains. Seasonal A(H1N1)pdm09 and A(H3N2) viruses and a less virulent A(H5N1) virus caused mild, nonfatal disease with limited or transient bloodwork changes in naïve ferrets. In contrast, naïve ferrets challenged with a highly virulent A(H5N1) virus showed virus detection beyond the upper respiratory tract, rapid disease progression accompanied by pronounced metabolic and biochemical disruption, necessitating humane euthanasia. Pre-existing immunity altered disease progression following challenge with this virus, with A(H1N1)pdm09-preimmune ferrets displaying reduced viral replication, less severe disease, and less pronounced biochemical disruption compared to A(H3N2)-preimmune ferrets. Overall, lymphopenia was common during acute infection in both ferret models; however, it did not distinguish nonfatal from fatal disease. Conversely, worsening biochemical changes, including hyperglycemia, increased alanine aminotransferase, total bilirubin, amylase, globulin, and electrolyte disturbances, were most evident in ferrets with severe A(H5N1) disease. These findings support the use of serial hematologic and serum chemistry analyses as complementary endpoints for evaluating disease severity, immune-mediated protection, and humane endpoint decisions in naïve and preimmune ferret models.

Pre-existing immunity altered disease progression following challenge with this virus, with A(H1N1)pdm09-preimmune ferrets displaying reduced viral replication, less severe disease, and less pronounced biochemical disruption compared to A(H3N2)-preimmune ferrets. Overall, lymphopenia was common during acute infection in both ferret models; however, it did not distinguish nonfatal from fatal disease. Conversely, worsening biochemical changes, including hyperglycemia, increased alanine aminotransferase, total bilirubin, amylase, globulin, and electrolyte disturbances, were most evident in ferrets with severe A(H5N1) disease. These findings support the use of serial hematologic and serum chemistry analyses as complementary endpoints for evaluating disease severity, immune-mediated protection, and humane endpoint decisions in naïve and preimmune ferret models.

papers.title: Towards influenza vaccine universality: Smart vaccine regimens and adjuvant-driven germinal center responses.
papers.abstract: Seasonal influenza vaccines are reformulated annually to match circulating strains of influenza A/H1N1, A/H3N2, and B, yet their efficacy remains fundamentally limited to neutralizing antibody responses against the strain-specific but highly variable hemagglutinin (HA) head domain. This limitation is compounded by pre-existing immunity, which preferentially recalls memory B cells targeting the predominant immune determinants, mainly the HA head domain, rather than the relatively conserved components. By contrast, conserved viral regions, including the HA stalk, neuraminidase (NA), the M2 ectodomain (M2e), and internal proteins such as nucleoprotein (NP) and matrix protein 1 (M1), are far less variable and represent attractive targets for broadly protective immunity. Developing an effective and affordable universal influenza vaccine hinges on solving two interconnected problems: redirecting germinal center (GC) selection toward conserved epitopes and programming immune responses for durable systemic and mucosal protection. This brief review highlights recent advances in antigen design, vaccination strategies, and adjuvant use. Together, these advances form a coordinated framework for developing a universal influenza vaccine.

papers.title: Assessing the impact of phylogenetic reconstruction error on genetic reassortment inference in segmented viruses.
papers.abstract: Recombination is an important process in the evolution of RNA viruses. For viruses with segmented genomes, recombination can occur by reassortment of entire genomic segments. This process has played a significant role in the adaptation and spread of influenza viruses with novel genomic combinations, i.e., antigenic shifts. Reassortment is usually identified by discrepancies between the topologies of trees reconstructed from different genomic segments, e.g., subtree prune and regraft (SPR) rearrangements. However, this phylogenetic discordance can also result from errors in tree reconstruction due to insufficient information. The objective of this study was to evaluate the contribution of phylogenetic reconstruction error to the inference of reassortment events from influenza A virus (IAV) genomes from avian hosts. We curated a dataset of 11,795 complete avian H5Nx IAV genomes and sampled subsets of HA sequences with different expected levels of reconstruction error. Next, we simulated molecular evolution along the trees reconstructed from these HA samples, varying rates of evolution and sequence lengths to correspond to the other genomic segments. Because these simulations had no reassortment, any phylogenetic discordance identified from the resulting trees must be caused by reconstruction error. We found that simulations from random samples yielded about 32% as many SPRs as obtained from real data. This false positive rate was reduced to 4% when simulating trees from the most genetically divergent subset of HA sequences. By modifying the simulated trees with SPR rearrangements, we observed a false negative rate of 8.5%, which increased with the number of SPRs per tree. Overall, we found that reassortment can be substantially overestimated from phylogenetic discordance, underscoring the need to account for phylogenetic uncertainty and sampling design when analyzing IAV datasets for reassortment.

papers.title: Mathematical AI Predicts 40% and 57% Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness Against H1N1 and H3N2, Respectively, for the 2026--2027 U.S. Season
papers.abstract: Background: Clinical influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) has often been low over the past two decades, highlighting the need for preseason VE forecasting. Timely forecasts could help health authorities plan prevention strategies and allocate healthcare resources. However, preseason forecasting of clinical influenza VE remains relatively uncommon. Methods: We obtained hemagglutinin (HA) sequences from GISAID for U.S. specimens collected in August--September before each influenza season from 2010--2011 through 2024--2025. After quality screening, we compared each virus with the corresponding vaccine target strain for the same season and subtype or lineage using two mathematical distances based on amino acid patterns in the HA protein. We calculated mean distances for each season and subtype or lineage and paired them with published clinical VE estimates, yielding 26 observations across 13 seasons. Using a mathematical AI approach, we fitted linear regression models of VE against each distance and evaluated their predictive performance by forecasting later seasons using data from earlier seasons, with the historical mean VE for each subtype or lineage as a reference. We then applied the same approach to 87 HA sequences collected in August--September 2026 to forecast VE for the 2026--2027 season. Results: We generated component-specific forecasts of influenza VE for the upcoming 2026--2027 U.S. Both mathematical distances were negatively associated with historical VE, indicating that greater differences between circulating viruses and vaccine strains were associated with lower VE. The topological model forecast VE of 40.3%, 56.9%, and 47.1% against A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria, respectively, whereas the geometric model forecast corresponding VE values of 34.0%, 56.8%, and 51.1%.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 在过去二十年中,临床流感 疫苗 有效性 (VE) 往往较低,这凸显了季前 VE 预测的必要性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 及时的预测可以帮助卫生当局规划预防策略并分配医疗资源。
elements_zh.methods: 我们从 GISAID 获得了 2010--2011 年至 2024--2025 年每个流感季节前 8 月至 9 月采集的美国样本的血凝素 (HA) 序列。经过质量筛选后,我们使用基于 HA 蛋白氨基酸模式的两个数学距离,将每种病毒与同一季节、亚型或谱系的相应 疫苗 目标毒株进行比较。我们计算了每个季节和亚型或谱系的平均距离,并将它们与已发表的临床 VE 估计值配对,在 13 个季节中产生了 26 个观察值。
elements_zh.main_results: 这两个数学距离均与历史 VE 呈负相关,表明流行病毒和 疫苗 毒株之间的较大差异与较低的 VE 相关。拓扑模型预测 甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09、甲型H3N2流感病毒 和 B/Victoria 的 VE 分别为 40.3%、56.9% 和 47.1%,而几何模型预测相应的 VE 值为 34.0%、56.8% 和 51.1%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 使用数学人工智能方法,我们针对每个距离拟合了 VE 线性回归模型,并通过使用早期季节的数据预测后期季节来评估其预测性能,并以每个亚型或谱系的历史平均 VE 作为参考。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现提供了一个预测框架,用于估计流感 疫苗 对特定亚型和谱系的有效性,这可以为 疫苗 毒株选择和公共卫生规划提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 所提供的证据并未报告该研究的局限性。

papers.title: Oseltamivir-Based Organic Salts and Ionic Liquids: Physicochemical Properties, Cytotoxicity, and Neuraminidase Inhibition
papers.abstract: Background: Neuraminidase (NA) inhibitors are widely used for the treatment of influenza, but the emergence of resistance and limitations in drug formulation can compromise their therapeutic performance. This study investigated whether counterion exchange can modulate the physicochemical properties, cytotoxicity, and NA-inhibitory activity of oseltamivir (OS) while preserving its covalent structure. Methods: Five OS-based ionic formulations, [OS][C1SO3], [OS][C3SO3], [OS][C6SO3], [OS][TolSO3], and [OS][CSA], were synthesized and characterized by NMR and ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, with isolated yields ranging from 84 to 88%. Spectroscopic data confirmed the formation of the desired 1:1 salts and showed that the OS ethyl ester remained chemically intact. The formulations were evaluated for aqueous solubility, octanol/water partitioning, cytotoxicity toward MDCK-SIAT1 cells, and NA-inhibitory activity using a MUNANA-based assay against NAs from A(H1N1)pdm09, its H275Y oseltamivir-resistant variant, A(H3N2), and type B influenza viruses. Results: All formulations exhibited low cytotoxicity, with CC50 values above 1200 μM. All OS ionic formulations showed lower IC50 values than oseltamivir phosphate against all four influenza viruses, with improvements ranging from approximately 2.5- to 393-fold. [OS][TolSO3] showed the highest potency, reducing the IC50 by approximately 336-fold against H275Y virus NA and 393-fold against influenza B virus NA. IC90 values showed the same overall potency ranking, although improvements at 50% inhibition were not always proportionally maintained at 90% inhibition. Conclusions: Overall, counterion selection substantially influenced both the physicochemical and biological profiles of OS. [OS][TolSO3] provided the highest NA-inhibitory potency, whereas [OS][CSA] exhibited the most balanced overall profile, supporting counterion engineering as a potential approach to optimize oseltamivir-based ionic formulations.

source_records.title: Oseltamivir-Based Organic Salts and Ionic Liquids: Physicochemical Properties, Cytotoxicity, and Neuraminidase Inhibition
source_records.abstract: Background: Neuraminidase (NA) inhibitors are widely used for the treatment of influenza, but the emergence of resistance and limitations in drug formulation can compromise their therapeutic performance. This study investigated whether counterion exchange can modulate the physicochemical properties, cytotoxicity, and NA-inhibitory activity of oseltamivir (OS) while preserving its covalent structure. Methods: Five OS-based ionic formulations, [OS][C1SO3], [OS][C3SO3], [OS][C6SO3], [OS][TolSO3], and [OS][CSA], were synthesized and characterized by NMR and ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, with isolated yields ranging from 84 to 88%. Spectroscopic data confirmed the formation of the desired 1:1 salts and showed that the OS ethyl ester remained chemically intact. The formulations were evaluated for aqueous solubility, octanol/water partitioning, cytotoxicity toward MDCK-SIAT1 cells, and NA-inhibitory activity using a MUNANA-based assay against NAs from A(H1N1)pdm09, its H275Y oseltamivir-resistant variant, A(H3N2), and type B influenza viruses. IC90 values showed the same overall potency ranking, although improvements at 50% inhibition were not always proportionally maintained at 90% inhibition. Conclusions: Overall, counterion selection substantially influenced both the physicochemical and biological profiles of OS. [OS][TolSO3] provided the highest NA-inhibitory potency, whereas [OS][CSA] exhibited the most balanced overall profile, supporting counterion engineering as a potential approach to optimize oseltamivir-based ionic formulations.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 神经氨酸酶 (NA) 抑制剂广泛用于流感 治疗,但耐药性的出现和药物配方的限制可能会影响其治疗效果。本研究调查了抗衡离子交换是否可以调节奥司他韦 (OS) 的理化性质、细胞毒性和 NA 抑制活性,同时保留其共价结构。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及使用 NMR 和 ATR-FTIR 光谱合成和表征五种基于 OS 的离子制剂:[OS][C1SO3]、[OS][C3SO3]、[OS][C6SO3]、[OS][TolSO3] 和 [OS][CSA]。评估了制剂的水溶性、辛醇/水分配、对 MDCK-SIAT1 细胞的细胞毒性,以及对来自 甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09、其 H275Y 奥司他韦抗性变体、甲型H3N2流感病毒 和 B 型流感病毒的 NA 的 NA 抑制活性。
elements_zh.methods: 这些制剂通过核磁共振和ATR-FTIR光谱法进行了合成和表征,其单独产率范围为84到88%。
elements_zh.main_results: 光谱数据证实了所需 1:1 盐的形成,并表明 OS 乙酯在化学上保持完整。所有制剂均表现出低细胞毒性,CC50 值高于 1200 μM。所有 OS 离子制剂对所有四种流感病毒的 IC50 值均低于磷酸奥司他韦,改善范围约为 2.5 至 393 倍。[OS][TolSO3] 显示出最高的效力,针对 H275Y 病毒 NA 的 IC50 降低了约 336 倍,针对乙型流感病毒 NA 的 IC50 降低了 393 倍。IC90 值显示出相同的总体效力排名,尽管 50% 抑制时的改善并不总是按比例维持在 90% 抑制时。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 总体而言,抗衡离子的选择极大地影响了 OS 的物理化学和生物学特征。[OS][TolSO3] 提供最高的 NA 抑制效力,而 [OS][CSA] 表现出最平衡的整体特征,支持反离子工程作为优化基于奥司他韦的离子制剂的潜在方法。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,抗衡离子工程可能是一种有前景的策略,可增强基于奥司他韦的离子制剂对 季节性流感 病毒 治疗 的治疗潜力,特别是在解决耐药性和提高药物溶解度和活性方面。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于体外评估,不包括体内或临床数据。证据是中等的,因为结果基于实验室实验,没有考虑现实世界的变异性或长期影响。

The Northern Hemisphere flu season is starting weeks ahead of schedule. The very beginning of the epidemic is caused by an H1N1 virus carrying a mutation that worries virologists and epidemiologists. This vaccine prepared for the 2026/2027 season has been rebuilt in all three of its components. Both facts point to the same advice: we should vaccinate earlier than usual, and the shot should not be a simple formality. The season is already running ahead of schedule, with influenza positivity unusually high for early autumn in the United Kingdom and on the United States (US) West Coast. In Japan, the exceptionally early outbreak observed already in August and early September provoked the closure of some schools.1 What is different about the virus? In the week ending September 26, 2026, H1N1 accounted for 96% of subtyped positive cases in the US, H3N2 for almost 4%, and influenza B was not detected, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) surveillance.2 This early-season subtype distribution contrasts with that observed during the previous influenza season, when H3N2 subclade K predominated. Sequencing points to a mutation in H1N1 called G155E. Alex Greninger’s laboratory at the University of Washington found it in 13 of 17 H1N1 samples from Seattle with sufficiently complete sequences. In a preprint from Jesse Bloom’s laboratory,3 antibodies in 260 blood samples from Australia and the US recognized some G155E-bearing strains less well, especially in sera from teenagers and young adults, who have probably not met similar H1N1 viruses before. The preprint has not yet been peer-reviewed. It measured pre-existing antibodies, not those produced by this year’s vaccine. And a handful of Seattle sequences is not a national picture. None of this is a reason for alarm; all of it is a reason for attention and further surveillance. Meanwhile, the vaccine for the 2026/2027 season has been rebuilt in all three components. The World Health Organization recommendation of February 27, 2026,4 replaces every strain. All vaccines carry an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus. Egg-based vaccines add A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2) and B/Tokyo/EIS13- 175/2025 (B/Victoria); cell-, recombinant- and nucleic-acid-based vaccines use A/ Darwin/1415/2025 and B/Pennsylvania/14/2025. The European Medicines Agency followed this recommendation.5 The choice was made in February 2026, 7 to 10 months before the season, as the Bloom preprint noted.3 That lead time is the structural weakness of egg- and cell-based manufacture: the virus keeps changing while the vaccine is being made. Whether the Journal of Clinical and Journal of Clinical and Translational Research Translational Research Editorial Volume x Issue x (2026) 2  doi: 10.36922/JCTR026420119 new H1N1 strain covers G155E-bearing viruses well is not something the sources available now settle, and it is too early to claim it. Laboratories will test it in the coming weeks, and agencies should publish those results promptly. None of this changes the case for vaccination. A vaccine that matches only partly still tends to protect better against severe disease than no vaccine, which is the outcome that fills hospital beds. The unusually early start to the season also calls for a second look at vaccination timing. The standard counsel has been to vaccinate in September or October, and to avoid July or August because immunity can wane over the season, especially in people aged 65 and over. CDC interim guidance for 2026–20276 keeps that logic, preferring completion by the end of October while encouraging vaccination for as long as viruses circulate. It is reasonable to consider receiving the influenza vaccine as soon as possible. The reason to delay was a possible loss of protection by February 2027. However, the reason to go now is an epidemic that may peak sooner than usual. Last year, Europe saw influenza detections three to four weeks earlier than in the two previous seasons. This year, it comes even faster. Anyone who has not yet been vaccinated, and above all those aged 65 and over, pregnant women, patients with chronic conditions, and health workers, should do so this month. Someone who got a shot in September need not do anything more, and CDC advises no booster dose for people already fully vaccinated this season. Alongside these timing concerns, new vaccine tools are emerging amid uncertainty surrounding the institutions responsible for vaccine guidance. A newly approved mRNA influenza vaccine is entering the US market for this season. On August 5, the Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna’s mFLUSIVA for adults aged 50–64 and granted accelerated approval for those aged 65 and over.7 It was tested in more than 20,000 adults. The attraction is speed. Whether mRNA shots deliver better protection in everyday use remains to be shown, and only real-world effectiveness data can judge that. The institutions that should help people choose among products are less settled. After the US Department of Health and Human Services replaced the members of the CDC vaccine advisory committee in June 2025, federal court orders halted implementation of that committee’s later votes, and CDC September 1 interim guidance says the July 2025 recommendations remain in effect for 2026–2027.8 The same guidance is silent on mFLUSIVA. Professional societies such as the American Academy of Family Physicians9 and the American Academy of Pediatrics10 have published their own recommendations. That helps, but it leaves clinicians, pharmacists, and patients, especially adults over 65, choosing between high- dose, adjuvanted, recombinant, and now mRNA products with less clarity than a season like this deserves. Against this backdrop, several immediate actions are warranted. The public should get vaccinated this month if eligible and not yet done. We should not wait for a better- matched product, because none is coming before the approaching season peak. Adults aged 65 and over should ask for a high-dose, recombinant, or adjuvanted vaccine where available, as CDC’s guidance prefers. Clinicians and pharmacies should prioritize older adults, pregnant patients, people with chronic conditions, and care staff, and say plainly that the vaccine is to prevent severe disease. Health agencies should publish early-season vaccine effectiveness estimates for H1N1 as soon as the data allow. They should report subtype and G155E frequency openly, so that everyone can follow the season as it unfolds. Regulators and advisory bodies should give clear, timely guidance on newer products such as mFLUSIVA, and restore a functioning, trusted process for national vaccine recommendations. Researchers should test whether antibodies induced by the 2026–2027 vaccines neutralize G155E viruses and share results as preprints within days, not months. The early signals may fade, and the season may prove ordinary. If they do not, the weeks ahead are the ones that count. Conflict of interest Jacek Z. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the early emergence of an H1N1 virus with a G155E mutation, which worries virologists and epidemiologists. The research aims to advise on earlier vaccination due to the unusual early start of the influenza season, with higher positivity rates observed in the UK and US.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involves surveillance of influenza cases in the US, with data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and sequencing data from Jesse Bloom’s laboratory. The study design includes the analysis of H1N1 samples from Seattle and blood samples from Australia and the US.
analysis.methods: Sequencing was performed to identify the G155E mutation in H1N1, and antibody recognition was tested in 260 blood samples from Australia and the US. The study also discusses the composition of the 2026/2027 influenza vaccine.
analysis.main_results: In the week ending September 26, 2026, H1N1 accounted for 96% of subtyped positive cases in the US, with no detection of influenza B. Sequencing points to the G155E mutation in H1N1, and antibodies in some samples recognized some G155E-bearing strains less well.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as a reason for attention and further surveillance, noting that the new H1N1 strain may not cover G155E-bearing viruses well. They emphasize the importance of vaccination, even if the vaccine is not fully matched to the circulating strain.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings caution against delaying vaccination, especially for high-risk groups such as those aged 65 and over, pregnant women, and health workers. The study highlights the need for timely vaccination and the importance of new vaccine tools.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study acknowledges the limitations of egg- and cell-based vaccine manufacturing, which can lag behind changes in the virus. The evidence strength is moderate due to the early stage of the season and the need for further testing of the vaccine against the new strain.

analysis.summary_en: The study highlights the early emergence of an H1N1 virus with a G155E mutation, advising earlier vaccination due to the unusual early start of the influenza season. Sequencing and antibody tests indicate reduced recognition of some G155E-bearing strains, emphasizing the need for timely vaccination and further surveillance.

papers.title: INFLUENZA SAZONAL: DIAGNÓSTICO, VIGILÂNCIA E PREVENÇÃO NA MEDICINA — UMA REVISÃO SISTEMÁTICA
papers.abstract: Introdução: A influenza sazonal é uma infecção respiratória aguda de circulação anual, responsável por elevada carga de hospitalizações, óbitos e custos aos sistemas de saúde. Objetivo: Sintetizar as evidências científicas publicadas entre 2021 e 2026 sobre diagnóstico, vigilância epidemiológica e prevenção da influenza sazonal. Metodologia: Revisão sistemática conduzida conforme as recomendações PRISMA 2020, com busca na base PubMed/MEDLINE por meio de estratégia booleana combinando descritores MeSH e termos livres relacionados à influenza humana, sazonalidade, diagnóstico, vigilância e vacinação. Dos 4.922 registros identificados, 70 estudos publicados entre 2021 e 2026 foram incluídos. Resultados: Os estudos foram agrupados em cinco eixos: aspectos clínicos e diagnósticos; vigilância epidemiológica, genômica e modelagem preditiva; efetividade e recomendações vacinais; novas plataformas vacinais, com destaque para as vacinas de RNA mensageiro; e cobertura vacinal, hesitação e grupos prioritários. A vacinação anual permanece como principal estratégia preventiva, embora sua efetividade varie conforme a temporada, o subtipo viral circulante e a faixa etária. A pandemia de COVID-19 alterou a dinâmica de circulação da influenza, incluindo o provável desaparecimento da linhagem B/Yamagata. Conclusão: O controle da influenza sazonal depende da integração entre diagnóstico laboratorial oportuno, vigilância sentinela e genômica contínua, vacinação anual com ampla cobertura e enfrentamento da hesitação vacinal, especialmente em gestantes, idosos, crianças e imunocomprometidos.

papers.title_zh: 流感季节:诊断、预防和医学预防 — UMA REVISÓ SISTEMÁTICA
papers.source_body_en: Introdução: A influenza sazonal é uma infecção respiratória aguda de circulação anual, responsável por elevada carga de hospitalizações, óbitos e custos aos sistemas de saúde. Objetivo: Sintetizar as evidências científicas publicadas entre 2021 e 2026 sobre diagnóstico, vigilância epidemiológica e prevenção da influenza sazonal. Metodologia: Revisão sistemática conduzida conforme as recomendações PRISMA 2020, com busca na base PubMed/MEDLINE por meio de estratégia booleana combinando descritores MeSH e termos livres relacionados à influenza humana, sazonalidade, diagnóstico, vigilância e vacinação. Dos 4.922 registros identificados, 70 estudos publicados entre 2021 e 2026 foram incluídos. Resultados: Os estudos foram agrupados em cinco eixos: aspectos clínicos e diagnósticos; vigilância epidemiológica, genômica e modelagem preditiva; efetividade e recomendações vacinais; novas plataformas vacinais, com destaque para as vacinas de RNA mensageiro; e cobertura vacinal, hesitação e grupos prioritários. A vacinação anual permanece como principal estratégia preventiva, embora sua efetividade varie conforme a temporada, o subtipo viral circulante e a faixa etária. A pandemia de COVID-19 alterou a dinâmica de circulação da influenza, incluindo o provável desaparecimento da linhagem B/Yamagata. Conclusão: O controle da influenza sazonal depende da integração entre diagnóstico laboratorial oportuno, vigilância sentinela e genômica contínua, vacinação anual com ampla cobertura e enfrentamento da hesitação vacinal, especialmente em gestantes, idosos, crianças e imunocomprometidos.
papers.abstract_zh: 简介: 流感是一种由呼吸道感染引起的每年循环的流感,可响应医院的紧急运输、系统和客户的要求。目标:作为 2021 年和 2026 年公共科学证据的科学诊断、流行病学警戒和流感区域预防。方法:修订 PRISMA 2020 推荐系统,以 PubMed/MEDLINE 为基础,结合 MeSH 和人类流感相关术语、诊断、诊断和警戒疫苗接种。包括 4.922 项注册登记、2021 年和 2026 年期间的 70 项公共研究。结果: 第五次研究中的孔洞研究:临床和诊断方面;流行病学、基因组和预测模型的警戒;有效和推荐疫苗;Novas vacinais 平台,com destaque para as vacinas de RNA mensageiro;疫苗接种、犹豫和优先事项。每年一次的永久性疫苗接种主要是预防性的,根据不同的情况采取不同的有效措施,以防止病毒循环和预防。COVID-19 的大流行改变了流感循环的动态,包括 B/Yamagata 地区的流行病。结论:流感的控制取决于实验室诊断的综合时机、警戒和持续的基因检测、每年的疫苗接种和疫苗接种的犹豫,特别是妊娠期、妊娠期和新生儿期的疫苗接种。免疫受损。

papers.full_text: Abstract Introduction This study aimed to assess attitudes and vaccination behaviors among primary healthcare workers toward seasonal influenza vaccination and to examine the psychological antecedents underlying their vaccination decisions using the Psychological Antecedents of Vaccination (5C) framework. Materials and Methods This cross-sectional study included 181 healthcare workers employed at primary healthcare institutions affiliated with a provincial health directorate. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to influenza vaccination, together with the seven-point Likert-type 5C scale. Participants who reported having received an influenza vaccine at least once in previous seasons were compared with those who had never been vaccinated. Participants were also compared according to their vaccination status during the 2025-2026 season. Variables showing significant associations in univariable analyses were subsequently entered into a multivariable binary logistic regression model. Results: The participants had a mean age of 38.1 ± 7.2 years, and 75.1% were women. Overall, 33.1% had received an influenza vaccine at least once, whereas only 16.6% had been vaccinated during the 2025-2026 season. Participants who had received an influenza vaccine at least once had higher collective responsibility scores (p = 0.045). Those vaccinated during the current season had lower constraints scores (p = 0.006) and higher calculation scores (p = 0.030). Introduction Influenza is a viral disease characterized by acute respiratory tract infection. The virus, which infects millions of people worldwide each year, causes approximately 290,000-650,000 deaths[1]. One in five unvaccinated children and one in ten unvaccinated adults contract seasonal influenza each year[2]. Although the symptoms of the disease can be mild, influenza can cause severe illness and death in high-risk individuals and is associated with high morbidity and mortality in children, older adults, individuals with chronic diseases, and pregnant women[1, 3]. Due to its high transmission rate and pandemic potential, influenza poses a significant public health risk. Seasonal influenza vaccination reduces the occurrence of severe symptoms and hospitalization by providing immunity against the disease[4, 5]. Healthcare workers are at a higher risk of seasonal influenza than other adults[6]. This occupational group, which plays a critical role in the nosocomial transmission cycle because of its close contact with infected patients, may transmit the virus to high-risk patients. Furthermore, significant workforce losses and associated economic burdens occur among healthcare personnel infected with seasonal influenza[7, 8]. Considering these risks, seasonal influenza vaccination for healthcare workers is recommended by authorities in many countries, and in some countries, it is mandatory for employment[9]. A recent survey of 34 European countries found that 33 have an influenza vaccination policy for healthcare personnel, and 16 mandate at least one vaccination for this group, with nine requiring vaccination as a prerequisite for employment[10]. In Türkiye, healthcare workers are among the risk groups for whom the seasonal influenza vaccine is provided free of charge, and vaccination is voluntary[11]. Despite recommendations from health authorities and the free provision of the vaccine, seasonal influenza vaccine uptake among healthcare workers remains low[12, 13]. In the most recent survey of European Union and European Economic Area countries, healthcare worker vaccination coverage was reported by only nine countries that recommended vaccination and ranged from 16.6% to 62.8%, with a median of 32%[14]. A systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the pooled influenza vaccine uptake among nurses at 44%[15], whereas coverage among healthcare personnel in the United States reached 76.3% in the 2024-2025 season[16]. Vaccine hesitancy is defined as a delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite the availability of vaccination services[17]. In studies examining seasonal influenza vaccine hesitancy among healthcare workers, factors such as doubts about vaccine effectiveness, concerns regarding vaccine safety, and a low perceived personal risk of influenza have emerged as prominent factors[18, 19]. Interventions designed to improve vaccine uptake have produced heterogeneous results, and their effectiveness appears to depend strongly on the behavior-change methods employed[20, 21]. In this context, identifying the underlying causes of vaccine hesitancy among healthcare workers and developing effective strategies to address them are critically important for reducing influenza cases among both healthcare personnel and the general public. The vaccine acceptance process is multidimensional, and the Psychological Antecedents of Vaccination (5C) model was developed by Betsch et al.[22]. The model conceptualizes vaccination decisions across five psychological dimensions: confidence, meaning trust in vaccines and the vaccination system; complacency, meaning a low perceived risk of vaccine-preventable diseases; constraints, meaning practical or psychological barriers to vaccination; calculation, meaning extensive searching for information about the risks and benefits of vaccination; and collective responsibility, meaning the willingness to protect others through one’s own vaccination[22]. This framework provides a comprehensive approach to understanding the psychological factors underlying vaccination decisions and has been shown to explain vaccination behavior better than sociodemographic variables alone[23]. The aim of this study is to determine the factors affecting the attitudes and vaccination behaviors of healthcare workers regarding the seasonal influenza vaccine. Furthermore, this study aimed to investigate the psychological processes underlying participants’ decisions to accept or reject the seasonal influenza vaccine based on the 5C model. Materials and Methods The population of this cross-sectional study consisted of physicians and allied healthcare personnel (midwives, nurses, health officers, medical secretaries, workers, and others) working at primary healthcare institutions affiliated with the İstanbul Provincial Health Directorate. The study aimed to reach the entire population (n = 222). To evaluate the applicability of the questionnaire developed by the researchers, a pilot study was conducted with 15 healthcare workers. The questionnaire, which was finalized after the pilot implementation, was administered using the supervised questionnaire method. This study was approved by İstanbul Medipol University Non-Interventional Clinical Research Ethics Committee (decision number: 1391, date: 13.11.2025). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before administration. Data were collected over two days, March 2 and 3, 2026, toward the end of the 2025-2026 influenza season, so that vaccination status for that season could be considered essentially complete at the time of data collection. A total of 181 healthcare workers actively working in primary care settings who fully completed the questionnaire were included in the study, corresponding to a response rate of 81.5%. Data Collection Tool The questionnaire, prepared by the researchers based on a literature review, consists of 18 questions divided into three sections and is provided in full, along with an English translation, in Supplementary File 1. Demographic information: This section consists of 10 questions regarding sociodemographic characteristics, such as age, sex, occupation, and educational status. Knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors regarding vaccination: This section included questions aimed at evaluating participants’ knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to vaccination. Vaccination training, influenza vaccine recommendation behavior, frequency of seasonal influenza vaccination, Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) vaccination status, and whether the vaccinations of participants’ children and/or first-degree relatives were complete were evaluated. Vaccination in previous seasons was assessed using a single item with three response options (vaccinated regularly every year, vaccinated occasionally but not regularly, or never vaccinated); participants who selected either of the first two options were classified as having been vaccinated at least once. Psychological antecedents of vaccination (5C) scale: The psychological antecedents of vaccination (5C) scale was developed by Betsch et al.[22] based on the World Health Organization’s 3C model[17]. The scale assesses five psychological antecedents that influence vaccination behavior. The confidence subdimension reflects trust in the effectiveness and safety of vaccines, the system that delivers them, and the motivations of policymakers; complacency reflects the perception that vaccine-preventable diseases pose a low risk and that vaccination is therefore unnecessary; constraints refer to perceived structural and psychological barriers that make vaccination difficult; calculation reflects the extent to which individuals engage in extensive information searching about the risks and benefits of vaccination; and collective responsibility reflects the willingness to protect others through one’s own vaccination[22]. Each subdimension consists of three items, and the scale comprises a total of 15 items. The items are rated on a seven-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). Therefore, each sub-dimension score ranges from 3 to 21, with higher scores indicating a stronger presence of the respective antecedent. In the original validation study, Cronbach’s alpha coefficients for the subdimensions ranged from 0.71 to 0.85, whereas values ranging from 0.71 to 0.82 were reported in the Turkish validity and reliability study[24]. In the original validation study, higher confidence scores were positively associated with vaccination behavior, whereas higher complacency and constraints scores were negatively associated with vaccination behavior; calculation and collective responsibility were not independent predictors in that sample. The calculation subdimension reflects individuals’ tendency to seek and evaluate information regarding the risks and benefits of vaccines[22]. Statistical Analysis Data analysis was performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences for Windows (version 27.0; Armonk, NY: IBM Corp., USA). Descriptive statistics are presented as frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations. The normality of numerical variables was assessed using skewness and kurtosis values. Categorical variables were compared using the Pearson chi-square test, and Fisher’s exact test was used when the minimum expected cell count was less than five. Student’s t-test and one-way analysis of variance were used to compare normally distributed numerical variables, and the Bonferroni test was used for post-hoc pairwise comparisons. For comparisons of the 5C subdimensions, professions were categorized into three groups: physicians, midwives/nurses, and other healthcare personnel (health officers, medical secretaries, workers, and others). For the binary logistic regression analysis, professions were dichotomized as physicians and non-physician healthcare workers. Sex, profession, and the behavior of recommending influenza vaccination, all of which were significant in univariable analyses, were entered into the primary multivariable binary logistic regression model using the enter method. Model fit was assessed using the omnibus test of model coefficients, the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, and the Nagelkerke R2 value. Odds ratios (ORs) were presented with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results A total of 181 of the 222 eligible healthcare workers completed the questionnaire, corresponding to a response rate of 81.5%. The participants had a mean age of 38.1 ± 7.2 years (range, 23-63 years), and 75.1% (n = 136) were women. A university degree or higher was reported by 77.9% (n = 141) of the participants. Of the participants, 17.1% (n = 31) were physicians or specialist physicians, 23.8% (n = 43) were midwives or nurses, and 59.1% (n = 107) belonged to other occupational groups. In addition, 60.8% (n = 110) were married, and 50.3% (n = 91) had children. Overall, 33.1% (n = 60) of the healthcare workers had received an influenza vaccine at least once, whereas only 16.6% (n = 30) had received the seasonal influenza vaccine during the 2025-2026 season. A COVID-19 vaccine had been received by 96.1% (n = 174) of the participants. Participants who had received an influenza vaccine at least once (n = 60) were compared with those who had never been vaccinated (n = 121) (Table 1). The proportion of women was significantly higher among participants who had been vaccinated at least once than among those who had never been vaccinated (85.0% vs. 70.2%, p = 0.031). Similarly, the proportions of physicians (28.3% vs. 11.6%, p = 0.005) and participants who recommended influenza vaccination to their close contacts (90.0% vs. 49.6%, p < 0.001) were significantly higher in the previously vaccinated group. No significant differences were observed between the two groups in age, educational level, marital status, having children, presence of chronic disease, presence of chronic disease in a first-degree relative, receipt of vaccination training, COVID-19 vaccination status, or completeness of vaccinations among their children and/or first-degree relatives. When the same characteristics were compared according to influenza vaccination status during the 2025-2026 season, no statistically significant association was observed with sex, educational level, marital status, having children, occupational group, presence of chronic disease, presence of chronic disease in a first-degree relative, or receipt of vaccination training (Supplementary Table 1). In contrast, participants who recommended influenza vaccination to their close contacts were significantly more likely to have received the influenza vaccine during the 2025-2026 season (p < 0.001). Furthermore, participants who had previously received an influenza vaccine at least once were significantly more likely to have received the vaccine during the 2025-2026 season than those who had never been vaccinated (p < 0.001). The 5C sub-dimension scores according to participant characteristics are presented in Table 2. No statistically significant differences were observed between women and men or between participants with different educational levels for any of the five subdimensions. Statistically significant differences were observed among occupational groups in the confidence, complacency, constraints, and collective responsibility sub-dimension scores (p = 0.002, p < 0.001, p = 0.002, and p = 0.022, respectively). Post-hoc comparisons showed that complacency and constraints scores were significantly higher among other healthcare personnel (health officers, medical secretaries, workers, and others) than among both physicians and midwives/nurses. In contrast, confidence scores were significantly lower among other healthcare personnel than among midwives/nurses. Although the overall analysis of variance for collective responsibility was statistically significant, none of the pairwise comparisons reached statistical significance after Bonferroni correction. Participants who had received the influenza vaccine during the 2025-2026 season had lower constraints scores (4.9 ± 2.3 vs. 6.8 ± 3.5, p = 0.006) and higher calculation scores (18.4 ± 2.9 vs. 16.8 ± 3.8, p = 0.030) than those who had not received the vaccine (Table 2). When collective responsibility sub-dimension scores were examined according to seasonal influenza vaccination status in previous seasons, the mean score was significantly higher among participants who had been vaccinated at least once than among those who had never been vaccinated (17.8 ± 3.8 vs. 16.7 ± 3.6, p = 0.045). No statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in the remaining four subdimensions. Participants who recommended the influenza vaccine to their close contacts had higher confidence scores (17.1 ± 3.8 vs. 14.4 ± 4.2, p < 0.001) and collective responsibility scores (18.2 ± 2.7 vs. 15.1 ± 4.2, p < 0.001) and lower complacency scores (7.1 ± 3.2 vs. 8.5 ± 3.6, p = 0.009) than those who did not recommend the vaccine (Table 2). analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the psychological processes influencing influenza vaccine acceptance among healthcare workers using the 5C model. It found that 33.1% of participants had received an influenza vaccine at least once, while only 16.6% were vaccinated during the 2025-2026 season. Significant differences in vaccine acceptance were observed across occupational groups, with physicians and women more likely to be vaccinated. The study highlights the importance of psychological factors such as collective responsibility and constraints in vaccine uptake. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal conclusions, and the evidence is considered moderate due to reliance on self-reported data. The findings suggest potential areas for targeted interventions to improve vaccination rates among healthcare workers.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在基于5C模型调查参与者决定接受或拒绝季节性流感 疫苗的心理过程。背景强调,流感是一种以急性呼吸道感染为特征的病毒性疾病。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 一项横断面研究针对 181 名在初级保健机构积极工作且完整填写问卷的医护人员进行。参与者的平均年龄为 38.1 ± 7.2 岁,其中 75.1% 为女性,17.1% 为医生或专科医生。
elements_zh.methods: 使用结构化问卷收集数据,评估与流感 疫苗接种 相关的社会人口特征、知识、态度和行为,以及七点李克特 5C 量表。在单变量分析中显示显着关联的变量随后被输入到多变量二元逻辑回归模型中。使用 Windows 社会科学统计包(版本 27.0)进行统计分析。
elements_zh.main_results: 总体而言,33.1% 的医护人员至少接种过一次 疫苗 流感疫苗,而在 2025-2026 季节期间只有 16.6% 的人接种过疫苗。至少接受过一次流感 疫苗 的参与者的集体责任感得分较高 (p = 0.045)。在当前季节接种疫苗的人具有较低的约束分数 (p = 0.006) 和较高的计算分数 (p = 0.030)。不同职业群体在自信、自满、约束和集体责任方面存在显着差异(分别为 p = 0.002、p < 0.001、p = 0.002 和 p = 0.022)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,无论是历史上还是 2025-2026 年季节,医护人员对流感 疫苗接种 的吸收率都很低。他们指出,推荐流感 疫苗接种 与 疫苗 接受程度独立相关。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the psychological processes underlying participants’ decisions to accept or reject the seasonal influenza vaccine based on the 5C model. The background highlights that influenza is a viral disease characterized by acute respiratory tract infection.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 181 healthcare workers actively working in primary care settings who fully completed the questionnaire. The participants had a mean age of 38.1 ± 7.2 years, with 75.1% being women and 17.1% being physicians or specialist physicians.
analysis_en.methods: Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to influenza vaccination, together with the seven-point Likert-type 5C scale. Variables showing significant associations in univariable analyses were subsequently entered into a multivariable binary logistic regression model. Statistical analysis was performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences for Windows (version 27.0).
analysis_en.main_results: Overall, 33.1% of the healthcare workers had received an influenza vaccine at least once, whereas only 16.6% had been vaccinated during the 2025-2026 season. Participants who had received an influenza vaccine at least once had higher collective responsibility scores (p = 0.045). Those vaccinated during the current season had lower constraints scores (p = 0.006) and higher calculation scores (p = 0.030). Significant differences across occupational groups were observed in confidence, complacency, constraints, and collective responsibility (p = 0.002, p < 0.001, p = 0.002, and p = 0.022, respectively).
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the uptake of influenza vaccination among healthcare workers was low, both historically and during the 2025-2026 season. They noted that recommending influenza vaccination was independently associated with vaccine acceptance.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform targeted interventions to improve influenza vaccine acceptance among healthcare workers, particularly by addressing psychological factors such as collective responsibility and constraints. They also highlight the importance of understanding occupational differences in vaccine uptake.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its cross-sectional design, which does not allow for causal inferences. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on self-reported data and a single survey, with potential biases related to response rates and participant recall.

papers.title: Genetic ancestry shapes context-dependent immune regulation across Indigenous South American populations
papers.abstract: Human immune responses remain poorly characterized across Indigenous South American (ISA) populations, limiting our understanding of human immune variation. Here, we generated a single-cell transcriptional atlas of 1.4 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 345 individuals representing 13 South American populations, profiled at baseline and following stimulation with lipopolysaccharide, influenza A virus, or Trypanosoma cruzi. Genetic ancestry was associated with the expression of a large fraction of the transcriptome, often only after stimulation, and explained more variation than age or sex. On average, cis-eQTLs accounted for one-quarter of these ancestry-associated differences. Thousands of regulatory variants were common in ISA populations but rare or absent in European reference datasets. Integrating eQTLs with GWAS revealed stimulation-specific disease-associated regulatory variants and an enrichment of ancestry-associated expression differences among genes with colocalizing signals. Our findings highlight the importance of studying diverse populations across immune contexts to understand the genetic architecture of human immune responses.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to understand immune variation across Indigenous South American populations by generating a single-cell transcriptional atlas of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 345 individuals. news.content: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk . Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-22-october-2026-week-43 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. The report is based on data up to week 42 of 2026 between 12 October and 18 October 2026. The main messages of this report are: Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity remained stable and is circulating at baseline levels. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like illness ( ILI ) increased slightly at seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents in the community decreased compared with the previous week. Weekly influenza vaccine uptake for the 2026 to 2027 season is reported for the third time this season. Data is for week 42 (up to 18 October 2026). Following issues with unavailable or incomplete influenza vaccination data at the time of analysis in weeks 41 and 42, several cohorts were not published in week 42. This has been corrected for this week’s report (week 43), and all cohorts are included. This will be corrected retrospectively in the report for week 42. There remains an issue that affects the attribution of vaccinations by provider setting, but is not expected to affect overall vaccination uptake estimates, which are considered to remain an accurate reflection of the influenza vaccination programme. Compared with the equivalent week last season (week 42 data, 2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower among patients aged 65 years and over (44.1% vs 49.3%), patients aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups (19.9% vs 22.1%), 2-year-olds (26.0% vs 26.9%), and 3-year-olds (25.8% vs 26.8%). In contrast, vaccine uptake is higher among pregnant women (26.0% vs 25.1%). COVID-19 activity showed mixed trends and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness increased slightly. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents increased compared with the previous week. By the end of week 42 2026 (week ending 18 October 2026) 33.9% of all people aged 75 years and over, and 14.8% of all people aged under 75 years with a weakened immune system, had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose since 1 October 2026. RSV activity showed mixed trends and is circulating at baseline levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis increased and were at seasonally expected levels. Note 1: these indicators use the moving epidemic method ( MEM ) and the mean standard deviation method ( MSD ) to define thresholds to determine their respective levels of activity. Further information on these methods can be found in Influenza surveillance in Europe: establishing epidemic thresholds by the Moving Epidemic Method and Setting thresholds to determine COVID-19 activity levels using the mean standard deviation ( MSD ) method, England, 2022 to 2024 . The MEM approach is well-established for some influenza surveillance indicators, however, for other indicators both the MEM and MSD are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to using MSD . These approaches will be considered alongside expert opinion and triangulation of other data sources. The Second Generation Surveillance System ( SGSS ) captures test result information for notifiable infectious diseases, including COVID-19 and influenza, from laboratories in England. The unified sample dataset ( USD ) stores all SARS-CoV-2 test results reported to SGSS , Respiratory DataMart and UKHSA laboratories, and is used to calculate the percentage of tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 among all SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted. As of 20 October 2026, there were a total of 1,915 COVID-19 cases identified in hospital settings in week 42, remaining stable compared with 2,007 cases in the previous week. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) PCR positivity in hospital settings remained stable in week 42, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 8.9% up to Sunday 18 October 2026 compared with 8.8% for the same period on the previous Sunday. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 13.4% up to Sunday 18 October 2026. This has remained stable compared with 13.7% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Note 2: data from previous seasons is aligned by day. Note 3: testing policy and practice may change over time which can impact positivity rates, therefore comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution. Notable changes in testing policy occurred during 2022 to 2023, which are outlined in the data quality report . Note 4: the highlighted line corresponds to the age group in the subplot title, grey lines correspond to all other age groups. Influenza positivity remained stable in week 42, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 6.3% up to Sunday 18 October 2026. This is compared with 6.2% on the previous Sunday. By type, influenza A positivity remained stable in week 42, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 5.5% up to Sunday 18 October 2026. Influenza B positivity decreased in the same week, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 0.2% up to Sunday 18 October 2026. Influenza A positivity rates were highest among those aged between 18 and 24 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 12.0% up to Sunday 18 October 2026. This has decreased from 16.8% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Influenza B positivity rates for the same period were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 2.4%. This has decreased from 3.0% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. RSV swab-positivity based PCR test results reported through SGSS have been included as a pilot indicator from week 49 2025 onwards. RSV positivity increased in week 42, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.1% up to Sunday 18 October 2026, compared with 0.7% up to the previous Sunday. RSV positivity rates were highest in those aged between 0 and 4 years with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 7.8% up to Sunday 18 October 2026 in week 42. This has increased from 4.5% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Respiratory DataMart is a sentinel laboratory-based surveillance system where participating laboratories report positive and negative test results for a number of respiratory viruses from samples primarily taken in hospital. A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 42, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 42, 3,856 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 231 positive samples for influenza: 143 influenza A (not subtyped), 13 influenza A (H3N2), 47 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 30 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity decreased slightly to 6.0% in week 42 compared with 6.3% in the previous week. In week 42, 4,586 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 331 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity decreased slightly to 7.2% compared with 8.1% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged 80 years and over at 10.2%. RSV positivity remained stable at 0.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 5.7%. Adenovirus positivity decreased slightly to 1.1%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 4.6%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity increased to 0.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 1.8%. Parainfluenza positivity increased to 3.4%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 9.4%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased slightly to 17.1%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 36.0%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 14 September 2026 and 27 September 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. Observations published from the WHO influenza vaccine composition meeting (VCM) in September 2026 suggest low reactivity of some viruses within the D.3.1.1 subclade with post-infection ferret antisera raised against A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus – the A(H1N1)pdm09 component in 2026 Southern and 2026/2027 Northern Hemisphere cell- and egg-based influenza vaccines - and human sera post-vaccination with the Southern Hemisphere vaccine 2026. It is not yet clear how vaccine effectiveness against clinical disease may be affected by these observations. Vaccines typically still provide protection against severe clinical disease when drifted strains are seen with only a modest reduction in effectiveness. The characterisation of circulating A(H3N2) viruses shows that A(H3N2) viruses are currently showing low genetic diversity. All sequenced viruses to date belong to genetic subclade K. To date, only a small number of influenza B viruses have been detected, which show some genetic diversity. Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 42 2026 (week ending 18 October 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 242 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 148 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 72 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 22 influenza B viruses. Details of the characterised viruses by subtype are shown in Tables 1, 2 and 3. The RVU has confirmed by genome sequencing the detection of live attenuated influenza vaccine ( LAIV ) viruses in 7 influenza A/B positive samples, collected from children aged between 2 and 16 years. UKHSA RVU performs antigenic characterisation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, influenza A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses using haemagglutination inhibition ( HI ) assays. Data from these assays are used to compare how similar the currently circulating influenza viruses are to the strains included in seasonal influenza vaccines, and to monitor for changes in circulating influenza viruses. Similarity of currently circulating influenza strains to vaccine strains is defined as having an antibody titre within 4-fold when compared with reference viruses representative of the vaccine strain. Antigenic characterisation of viruses in the current reporting period is underway. A(H1N1)pdm09: 5 A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses have been antigenically characterised and 3 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H1N1)pdm09 vaccine strains. Influenza positive samples are screened for mutations in the virus neuraminidase ( NA ) and the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein (PA) genes known to confer neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir and zanamivir) or baloxavir resistance, respectively. Results from this surveillance are given in table 4. There have been less than 5 detections with mutations related to reduced susceptibility/resistance to oseltamivir and/or reduced susceptibility to baloxavir. Data is presented on viral ARI incidents in different settings that are reported to UKHSA health protection teams ( HPTs ). Please note that reporting practices are known to vary between seasons and between regions. Any interpretation of temporal and regional trends should consider the likelihood of differences in reporting of ARI incidents over time and between regions. There were 135 new ARI incidents reported in week 42 in England. These included: 124 incidents from care homes, of which 43 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 11 were due to influenza A, 3 were due to influenza (no type information available), 3 were due to multiple pathogens, 1 was due to RSV and 1 was due to other pathogens. No pathogen was reported in 62 incidents 6 incidents from hospitals, of which 4 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 1 was due to influenza A and 1 was due to multiple pathogens 2 incidents from educational settings, of which 1 was due to RSV . No pathogen was reported in 1 incident 1 incident from prisons, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 2 incidents from other settings, of which 1 was due to SARS-CoV-2 and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available) Syndromic surveillance collects data from various healthcare sources where presentations are classified by patterns of symptoms compatible with specific infections. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. Further details and data from other syndromic surveillance systems can be found in the syndromic surveillance weekly summaries . During the week ending on 18 October 2026, ED attendances for acute respiratory infections increased and were similar to seasonally expected levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness increased. ED attendance for influenza-like illness increased and was above seasonally expected levels. ED attendance for acute bronchiolitis (a syndrome related to RSV infection) increased and was below seasonally expected levels. Daily NHS 111 acute respiratory infection triaged calls showed small increases. GP in-hours COVID-19-like consultation rate continued to increase, mainly in those aged 65 years and over. Upper respiratory tract infections remained stable overall however there was a further small increase in influenza-like illness ( ILI ), which remained above seasonal expectations. ILI rates increased in adult age groups over 45 years. GP out-of-hours daily contacts for acute respiratory infections stabilised and remained in line with seasonally expected levels. Contacts for ‘difficulty breathing, wheeze, or asthma’ decreased but remained above seasonally expected levels. Note 6: 7-day moving average is adjusted for bank holidays. Grey columns show weekends and bank holidays. Note 7: the coloured line is the 7-day moving average by age group. Grey lines show the other age groups. The y-axis shows daily attendances. It is adjusted for bank holidays. Primary care surveillance is undertaken in collaboration with the Royal College of General Practitioners ( RCGP ) Research and Surveillance Centre ( RSC ), using a national sentinel surveillance system of around 2,000 GP practices covering over 20 million registered patients of all ages across England. More information on the methodology can be found in the data quality report . The weekly ILI consultation rate through the RCGP surveillance remained stable at 6.5 per 100,000 registered population in participating GP practices in week 42 compared with 6.3 per 100,000 in the previous week. This rate is in the baseline activity level (Figure 20). By age group, the highest rates were seen in those aged between 15 and 44 years (7.6 per 100,000), and those aged between 45 and 64 years (7.0 per 100,000). The lower respiratory tract infections ( LRTI ) consultation rate remained stable at 81.9 per 100,000 in week 42. Further details are available in the weekly RSC communicable and respiratory disease report for England . MEM thresholds are based on data from the 2018 to 2019 season to the 2025 to 2026 season. Note the 2019 to 2020, 2020 to 2021 and 2021 to 2022 seasons have been removed. From week 40 2025, the RCGP sentinel swabbing scheme testing capability has been expanded to the UKHSA Bristol laboratory in addition to the UKHSA Colindale laboratory. Samples sent to Colindale are tested for influenza A and B, RSV A and B, SARS-CoV-2, hMPV , adenovirus, seasonal coronavirus and enterovirus/rhinovirus while samples sent to Bristol are tested for influenza A and B, RSV and SARS-CoV-2. 931 samples were taken in…

This has decreased from 16.8% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. RSV positivity rates were highest in those aged between 0 and 4 years with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 7.8% up to Sunday 18 October 2026 in week 42. This has increased from 4.5% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Respiratory DataMart is a sentinel laboratory-based surveillance system where participating laboratories report positive and negative test results for a number of respiratory viruses from samples primarily taken in hospital. A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 42, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 42, 3,856 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 231 positive samples for influenza: 143 influenza A (not subtyped), 13 influenza A (H3N2), 47 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 30 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity decreased slightly to 6.0% in week 42 compared with 6.3% in the previous week. In week 42, 4,586 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 331 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity decreased slightly to 7.2% compared with 8.1% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged 80 years and over at 10.2%. RSV positivity remained stable at 0.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 5.7%. Adenovirus positivity decreased slightly to 1.1%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 4.6%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity increased to 0.5%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 1.8%. Parainfluenza positivity increased to 3.4%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 9.4%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased slightly to 17.1%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 36.0%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 14 September 2026 and 27 September 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. Observations published from the WHO influenza vaccine composition meeting (VCM) in September 2026 suggest low reactivity of some viruses within the D.3.1.1 subclade with post-infection ferret antisera raised against A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus – the A(H1N1)pdm09 component in 2026 Southern and 2026/2027 Northern Hemisphere cell- and egg-based influenza vaccines - and human sera post-vaccination with the Southern Hemisphere vaccine 2026. It is not yet clear how vaccine effectiveness against clinical disease may be affected by these observations. Vaccines typically still provide protection against severe clinical disease when drifted strains are seen with only a modest reduction in effectiveness. To date, only a small number of influenza B viruses have been detected, which show some genetic diversity. Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 42 2026 (week ending 18 October 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 242 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 148 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 72 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 22 influenza B viruses. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. news.title_original: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 22 October 2026 (week 43) - GOV.UK

analysis.time: The report covers data up to week 42 of 2026, between 12 October and 18 October 2026, with the publication date being 22 October 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The report is focused on England, with data on influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 activity across different age groups and populations, including those aged 75 years and over, individuals with weakened immune systems, and school-aged children.
analysis.event: The report outlines the current status of influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 activity in England, noting stable influenza activity, mixed trends for RSV, and low-level circulation of COVID-19. It also discusses vaccine uptake data and testing methodologies.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Influenza activity remained stable and at baseline levels. ED attendances for influenza-like illness increased slightly. The number of influenza-confirmed ARI incidents decreased compared with the previous week. Vaccine uptake was lower among certain age groups and clinical risk groups compared to the previous season, but higher among pregnant women. RSV activity showed mixed trends and was at baseline levels. COVID-19 activity showed mixed trends, with stable hospital cases and a slight increase in ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report indicates that influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to MSD. There were issues with incomplete vaccination data in weeks 41 and 42, but these were corrected in week 43. The methods used are experimental and may be subject to future revision. The unified sample dataset (USD) is used to calculate SARS-CoV-2 test positivity rates, and the data is considered accurate for overall vaccination uptake estimates.

analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 22 October 2026 (week 43) provides an overview of influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 activity in England. Influenza activity remained stable, with ED attendances for influenza-like illness increasing slightly. The number of influenza-confirmed ARI incidents decreased compared to the previous week. Vaccine uptake for the 2026-2027 season was lower among older adults, clinical risk groups, and young children, but higher among pregnant women. RSV activity showed mixed trends and was at baseline levels. COVID-19 activity was also mixed, with stable hospital cases and a slight rise in ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness. The report notes that influenza surveillance has shifted from MEM to MSD, and data quality issues in earlier weeks were resolved. The USD dataset is used for SARS-CoV-2 positivity calculations, and overall vaccination uptake estimates are considered accurate despite some methodological challenges.

news.title_zh: 国家流感和 COVID-19 监测 报告:2026 年 10 月 22 日(第 43 周) - GOV.UK
news.source_body_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 22 October 2026 (week 43) provides an overview of influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 activity in England. Influenza activity remained stable, with ED attendances for influenza-like illness increasing slightly. The number of influenza-confirmed ARI incidents decreased compared to the previous week. Vaccine uptake for the 2026-2027 season was lower among older adults, clinical risk groups, and young children, but higher among pregnant women. RSV activity showed mixed trends and was at baseline levels. COVID-19 activity was also mixed, with stable hospital cases and a slight rise in ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness. The report notes that influenza surveillance has shifted from MEM to MSD, and data quality issues in earlier weeks were resolved. The USD dataset is used for SARS-CoV-2 positivity calculations, and overall vaccination uptake estimates are considered accurate despite some methodological challenges.
news.content_zh: 2026 年 10 月 22 日(第 43 周)的全国流感和 COVID-19 监测 报告概述了英格兰的流感、RSV 和 COVID-19 活动。流感活动保持稳定,因流感样疾病急诊就诊的人数略有增加。与前一周相比,流感确诊病例数量有所减少。2026-2027 年季节,老年人、临床风险群体和幼儿的 疫苗 摄入量较低,但孕妇的摄入量较高。RSV 活性呈现出混合趋势,且处于基线水平。COVID-19 活动也好坏参半,医院病例稳定,急诊室因 COVID-19 类疾病就诊的人数略有增加。报告指出,流感 监测 已从 MEM 转向 MSD,并且前几周的数据质量问题得到了解决。USD 数据集用于 SARS-CoV-2 阳性计算,尽管存在一些方法学挑战,但总体 疫苗接种 吸收估计被认为是准确的。
